Microgravity materials research

Metal doesn't freeze
the same way off Earth.

Space-Cryo is building a CubeSat-scale thermal processing system that controls how eutectic alloys solidify in microgravity — turning a $100K, once-a-decade ISS experiment into a repeatable one.

The problem

Space manufacturing research is rare, expensive, and hard to repeat.

Buoyancy-driven convection doesn't exist in orbit, which changes how alloys crystallize — but almost nobody can test that directly, and Earth-based simulations only go so far.

01

Space experiments cost too much and fly too rarely to build real datasets.

02

Ground-based tests can't replicate true microgravity solidification behavior.

03

The result is a data gap holding back the next generation of in-space manufacturing.

How it works

A satellite-deployed lab for controlled freezing.

STEP 01
Melt, in a sealed chamber
A eutectic alloy sample sits in the "Thermal Heart" — a compact chamber ringed by four cartridge heaters capable of reaching 500°C, monitored by PT100 RTD sensors.
STEP 02
Drive a directional gradient
A thermoelectric cooler on the opposite end pulls heat away, establishing a controlled 20–50°C gradient. A stepper-driven linear actuator translates the sample through it at a set rate.
STEP 03
Log, repeat, compare
Closed-loop PID control and continuous RTD feedback keep every run repeatable, with full data logging for post-test microstructure analysis — on the ground or in orbit.
